rmt-2008-power-01.prompt:
*Setup.* A *knot diagram* is a closed loop in the plane that may cross itself, with a gap left at each crossing to show which arc passes over and which under (only two arcs cross at any point). Two diagrams are *equivalent* if one can be turned into the other by a sequence of the *Reidemeister moves*: R0 (deform the picture in the plane without changing the crossings), RI (add or remove a small kink, a loop with one crossing), RII (slide one strand completely over, or under, another, creating or removing two crossings) and RIII (slide a strand over or under the crossing of two other strands, across a small triangle of three crossings). The moves may be applied to rotated versions of the local pictures. A *knot invariant* (or *link invariant*) is a quantity that is the same for equivalent knots (links). For $i<j$ the result of problem $i$ may be used in problem $j$.

Show that the R-moves imply the first two of the *reverse R-moves* shown in the figure: RI$_2$ (removing a kink of the opposite handedness to the kink of RI) and RIII$_2$ (a version of RIII with a different over/under arrangement of the three crossings). (The remaining reverse moves may be used without proof later.)
rmt-2008-power-01.answer: RI$_2$: RI then RII. RIII$_2$: RII, RIII, RII.
rmt-2008-power-01.reviewNote: Figure-based proof: the official solution is a chain of diagrams; the solution here describes the sequence of moves (RI, RII for RI2; RII, RIII, RII for RIII2) in words, so a human should compare with the pictures.

The moves may be applied to rotated versions of the local pictures. A *knot invariant* (or *link invariant*) is a quantity that is the same for equivalent knots (links). For $i<j$ the result of problem $i$ may be used in problem $j$.

*Kauffman bracket.* For an unoriented link diagram $D$ the Kauffman bracket $\langle D\rangle$ is a polynomial in $A,A^{-1}$ defined by: it is invariant under R0 moves; $\langle U\rangle=1$ for the crossingless unknot; $\langle D\sqcup U\rangle=(-A^2-A^{-2})\langle D\rangle$ when a crossingless unknotted loop $U$ is added disjointly; and, at any crossing, $\langle D\rangle=A\langle D_+\rangle+A^{-1}\langle D_-\rangle$ where $D_+$ and $D_-$ are obtained by replacing the crossing by the two smoothings shown in the figure (the over-strand of the crossing is the one going from lower left to upper right; the left smoothing in the figure is the one with coefficient $A$).

*Writhe and Jones polynomial.* For an oriented link diagram $D$, the *writhe* $w(D)$ is the sum of the signs of all its crossings (the same as the linking number but with self-crossings counted as $\pm1$ instead of $0$). The *Jones polynomial* is $f_D(A)=(-A^3)^{-w(D)}\langle D\rangle$.

The connect sum $D_1\#D_2$ of two oriented diagrams is formed by cutting each in a single place (on an arc, away from crossings) and joining the ends so that the orientations match, producing a single diagram with $D_1$ and $D_2$ in disjoint discs. Reflecting a three-dimensional knot across a plane flips all the crossings of the corresponding two-dimensional diagram (the arc that was on top goes to the bottom, and vice versa). A knot is called *amphichiral* if it is equivalent to its mirror image, and *chiral* if it is not. Find a method for determining whether a (2D) knot is amphichiral or chiral. Is the trefoil knot chiral?
rmt-2008-power-17.answer: Replacing $A$ by $A^{-1}$ in the Jones polynomial gives the mirror image's polynomial; an amphichiral knot has $f(A)=f(A^{-1})$. The trefoil is chiral.
